name.canonical: Academic Cartography, Robinson School — Mid–Late 20th Century
name.inspiration_notice: An unofficial interpretive brief derived from source research and intended to guide original map styling; it does not reproduce or imply endorsement by referenced institutions, publishers, or cartographers.
organization_or_origin: Office of Strategic Services wartime antecedent

description.summary: A rational, restrained, communication-first academic style: maps are not decorative pictures but carefully balanced graphic arguments. The look is clean, moderate, legible, and purposefully hierarchical, often with cream or white backgrounds, fine black/gray linework, disciplined type, limited color, clear classification, and marginal information that documents projection, scale, data, date, and authorship.
description.design_principle: Every visible element should be integrated into a single communicative unit: clear enough to read, ordered enough to teach from, and restrained enough that no symbol is more or less prominent than its role requires.
description.historical_context: Robinson helped transform American cartography from craft drafting into an academic design-and-communication discipline. The style should evoke a UW–Madison classroom/lab product from the 1950s–1970s: hand-drafted or mechanically reproduced, intellectually disciplined, methodologically explicit, and designed around the reader as map percipient. black-and-white textbook reproduction two-color instructional figures offset lithography

behavior: Design first in grayscale; add color only when it strengthens communication.
Prefer two-color figures: black/gray plus one muted hue.
Use ordered lightness steps for quantitative data; hue changes only when categories truly differ.
Represent uncertainty with gray screens, dashed outlines, or stipple rather than saturated warning colors.
Use color as part of symbol hierarchy, not as decoration.
avoid: neon cyan, magenta, lime, and dashboard blue
faux antique browns that imply a much older parchment map

typography.character: Bookish, disciplined serif/sans mix. Titles may use a classic serif or sober transitional serif; labels should use compact legible serif or humanist sans. Type should feel typeset, not hand-lettered or corporate-app-like.
typography.fallback_strategy: Prefer metrically stable, licensable fonts with the language coverage required by the map; preserve hierarchy when substitution is necessary.
rules: Never use more than two font families.
Italicize hydrographic labels; use letterspacing for large-area labels.
Keep labels horizontal where possible, except water/linear features.
Use type placement to clarify figure-ground, not to decorate.
Do not use drop shadows, glows, novelty fonts, script fonts, or condensed tech-dashboard type.
Use title, subtitle, legend, notes, and sources as a coherent marginal information system.

linework: Precise ink-drafted strokes: thin, consistent, and hierarchical. Use hairline graticules, slightly stronger coastlines, and moderated administrative boundaries.
coastlines: 0.8–1.1 px dark gray/black with subtle water/land contrast
international or state boundaries: 0.6–0.9 px black or gray; use dashes only for disputed/secondary boundaries
study-area boundary: slightly heavier black or oxide-red rule, never glowing
water bodies filled pale blue with darker fine outlines only where needed
rivers drawn as tapered or hierarchy-weighted blue-gray lines
minor streams omitted at small scales
roads/railroads appear only when analytically relevant
railroads may use fine black line with short tick/cased pattern in OSS-inspired intelligence maps
major roads should be understated gray or tan lines; no bright shield-heavy highway basemap
use contours, hillshade, or hypsometric tints only if the theme needs terrain
relief should be subtle, low-contrast, and subordinate to thematic data
avoid Raisz-style physiographic hill drawings unless explicitly requested as a hybrid

required: Every visible element should be integrated into a single communicative unit: clear enough to read, ordered enough to teach from, and restrained enough that no symbol is more or less prominent than its role requires.
preferred: Use Robinson projection for general world maps when stylistically appropriate.
Use Albers, Lambert conformal conic, or another academically defensible projection for regional maps when Robinson would be inappropriate.
State projection, data source, date, units, and classification method in marginalia or source modal.
Design the map to work as a static figure before adding interactions.
Use restrained color and typography, with clear visual hierarchy.
Generalize data to the display scale; avoid over-detailed geometry.
Do not overload the map with labels merely because data are available.
In MapLibre/web map library, suppress default controls or restyle them as small square cream buttons with thin borders.
Implement hatch/stipple via SVG patterns or Canvas pattern fills for missing/uncertain areas.
Use D3 or chroma-like logic to build lightness-ordered ramps; verify contrast in grayscale.
For world maps in MapLibre, use preprojected GeoJSON/SVG if Robinson projection is required and native projection support is insufficient.

accessibility.color_independence: Sequential ramps must remain interpretable in grayscale. Use lightness, texture, and line style redundantly; do not rely on red/green distinction alone.
accessibility.contrast: Preserve readable contrast for labels, lines, and critical symbols at intended zoom levels.
accessibility.minimum_text_size: Adapt historical or print typography to a practical screen-reading threshold.
additional: Test the compiled style in grayscale and under common color-vision simulations.
